title: How do you decide what price a client should charge?
description: "What price should the client charge?" Setting or changing a price. The structure, the first question to ask, and practice prompts with model answers.
hook: Pricing cases can feel slippery, because there is no single right price. The way through is to look at it from three sides: what it costs, what customers would pay, and what rivals charge. Here is how.
body:
When you will use it

Setting or changing a price.

This is a generate question: "How can we do this?" Lay out every option in buckets that don't overlap, size them, then pick the best few. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What is the goal: profit, market share, or getting in fast?

One good question at the start can halve the work. It tells you where to look, and it shows the interviewer you are thinking about the client, not reciting a list.

The structure

  • Floor: our costs
    • Variable cost per unit (stay above it, unless it is a deliberate loss leader)
    • Fixed costs and investment (recovered over expected volume)
  • Ceiling: value to the customer
    • Price of their next best option
    • Extra value we add (savings · more revenue for them)
  • Reference: the alternatives (sit above or below them?)
    • Competitor prices
    • Substitutes

Say it out loud as a short sentence per branch, then say which branch you would look at first and why. That last part, your hypothesis, is what most candidates forget.

Make it your own

Cost sets the floor, value to the customer sets the ceiling, and the alternatives tell you where to land in between. Then check the effect on your other products.

Interviewers can tell when a structure has been memorised. Swap the general words for words about this client: not "costs", but "fuel and crew costs" for an airline.

Practise with real prompts

Read each prompt, take two minutes to sketch your own structure, then compare.

1. What price should a company charge for fast EV charging?

Show a model structure
  • Cost floor: Electricity, grid fees, equipment per kWh; Utilisation needed to break even
  • Customer value: Cost of charging at home vs on the road; Time saved, convenience
  • Competitors: Rivals' prices, subscriptions; Fuel cost per mile as a reference
  • Structure: Per kWh, per minute, subscription; Peak and off-peak

Where to start: Cost floor vs value ceiling: price sits between the two.

The trap: Copying rivals' prices without knowing your own cost and utilisation.

2. Should an electronics retailer introduce a price-match guarantee?

Show a model structure
  • Customer impact: Extra sales from confidence; Share of customers who would claim
  • Cost: Margin given up on matched sales; Admin to check claims
  • Competitor response: Rivals matching back, price war; Online-only rivals
  • Rules: Which rivals and products; In-store vs online

Where to start: Cost: how many sales would be matched, and at what discount.

The trap: Assuming only a few customers will claim.

3. Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show a model structure
  • Acquisition: New users attracted; Conversion from free to paid
  • Cannibalisation: Paying users moving down; What the free plan leaves out
  • Costs: Hosting and support for free users; Fraud and abuse
  • Competition: Rivals' free plans; How customers choose a tool

Where to start: Conversion from free to paid vs paying users who downgrade.

The trap: Counting sign-ups as success.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. You can see this tree drawn step by step, and every other core framework, on the free frameworks page.
